rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God wills ease by granting the sick and traveler a concession to break the fast.
rows.anchor: أي: بالرخصة للمسافر والمريض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusr means ease; yasar (wealth or abundance) is so called because it makes affairs easier.
rows.anchor: معناه: السهولة، ومنه يقال للغنى والسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The left hand is said either to be named optimistically for ease or because it helps the right hand make tasks easier.
rows.anchor: قيل: على التفاؤل باليسر، وقيل: لأنه يتسهل الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not will hardship because He has not imposed severity or restriction on you.
rows.anchor: لأنه لم يشدد ولم يضيق عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affirmation and negation of divine will here concern legal rulings for Muslims.
rows.anchor: وهذه الإرادة ونفي الإرادة تختص بالأحكام لأهل الإسلام

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: God intends His command to fast to be easy for you, not difficult.
rows.anchor: قال الحسين بن الفضل: يريد الله أن يكون أمره بالصوم عليكم ميسرا

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: A period of days is called an ʿidda; Abu Zayd says a man’s ʿidda ends when his appointed term ends.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد: يقال انقضت عدة الرجل إذا انقضى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Through ʿAta, Ibn Abbas says to complete the month’s days exactly: thirty if it has thirty, twenty-nine if it has twenty-nine.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: ولتكملوا عدة أيام الشهر، إن كان ثلاثين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih says to make up each missed day with one day.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه أيضا يعني: عدة ما أفطرتم، يوما مكان يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In both reports, Ibn Abbas interprets completing the count as making up Ramadan fasts.
rows.anchor: فحمل ابن عباس إكمال العدة في الروايتين على قضاء رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the make-up reading, the conjunction follows the sense rather than wording: the concession eases matters so people can complete the count after recovery or returning home.
rows.anchor: العطف على معنى الكلام لا على ظاهر اللفظ، وذلك أن في إباحته الإفطار للمريض والمسافر تسهيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may coordinate according to intended meaning; al-Zajjaj’s cited poetry supplies an example of coordination by sense.
rows.anchor: بادت وغير آيهن مع البلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari supports coordination by sense with a poem: if snakes spare a foot, the foot has spared them too.
rows.anchor: قد سالم الحيات منه القدما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis coordinates the phrase with an omitted earlier purpose clause: God wills ease and does not will hardship, to make people happy and let them complete the count.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون الواو عاطفة على مضمر في الكلام

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ instead treats the waw as resumptive and the lām as governed by an omitted verb: God granted the concession so people would make up missed fasts.
rows.anchor: واختار الفراء هذا القول، وقال: معنى الآية: ولتكملوا العدة في قضاء ما أفطرتم، والواو واو استئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ compares the omitted verb to God showing Abraham the kingdoms so that he would become certain.
rows.anchor: وكذلك نري إبراهيم ملكوت السماوات والأرض وليكون من

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says the phrase means completing the month’s days, implying performance rather than make-up.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أيضا ما يدل على أن المراد بإكمال العدة إكمالها في الأداء لا في القضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand completing the count as making up missed fasts.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون على أن المراد به إكمال العدة في القضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light form is supported by the verse today I have perfected your religion and Imruʾ al-Qays’s poetic usage.
rows.anchor: فمن خفف فلقوله: {اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form is valid because faʿʿala and afʿala often alternate; al-Nabigha’s verse is another example.
rows.anchor: ومن شدد فلأن فعل وأفعل يتعاقبان في أكثر الأحوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is purposive, not imperative; an imperative lām after waw, fa, or thumma may be vowelless, as in the two readings of the Hajj verse.
rows.anchor: لام كي (¬2)، وليست لام الأمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s report, Ibn Abbas says to magnify God for the religious laws to which He guided you.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: يريد لتعظموا الله على. ما أرشدكم له من شرائع الدين

rows.speaker: أكثر العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars understand this as the takbir on the night of Eid al-Fitr.
rows.anchor: أكثر العلماء (¬6): أراد به التكبير ليلة الفطر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Muslims are obliged to pronounce takbir when they see the Shawwal crescent.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في هذه الآية: حق على المسلمين إذا رأوا هلال

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak relates that Adam landed in India and Eve in Jeddah; after searching, they met and recognized one another at Arafat, naming the day ʿArafa and the place ʿArafat.
rows.anchor: فقال الضحاك: إن آدم عليه السلام لما أهبط، وقع بالهند

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta says Gabriel showed Abraham the rites, repeatedly asking whether he recognized them; the place was named ʿArafat from this exchange.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: إن جبريل عليه السلام كان يري إبراهيم المناسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God at the Sacred Monument means supplication and talbiya at Muzdalifah, also called Jamʿ because the evening prayers are combined there.
rows.anchor: فاذكروا الله} أي: بالدعاء والتلبية (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The place is called mashʿar from shiʿar, a sign, because it marks Hajj; prayer, standing, lodging, and supplication there are rites.
rows.anchor: وتسمى مشعرا من الشعار، وهو العلامة؛ لأنه معلم الحج.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf is accusative; remember God with a remembrance corresponding to His guidance, as requital for that guidance.
rows.anchor: موضع الكاف نصب. المعنى: واذكروه ذكرا مثل هدايته إياكم، أي: يكون جزاء لهدايته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God means affirming His oneness, praising Him, and thanking Him.
rows.anchor: ومعنى (اذكروه) بتوحيده والثناء عليه والشكر له

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh gives dhikran as a verbal noun like hifẓan, and notes dhikran alongside shirban.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: يقال: ذكرته ذكرا مثل: حفظته حفظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr can mean remembering, as opposed to forgetting; the cited example is Moses’s companion saying Satan made him forget the fish.
rows.anchor: فمما هو خلاف النسيان قوله: {وما أنسانيه إلا الشيطان أن أذكره}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr can also mean speech, whether speech that does not disparage its subject or speech that does; the latter is illustrated by a report about disparaging idols.
rows.anchor: والذكر الذي هو قول يستعمل على ضربين: قول لا ثلب فيه للمذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAdi ibn Hatim’s line uses yadhkurukum to mean disparage you.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قول الشاعر: يذكركم منا عدي بن حاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikra is also used as a verbal noun for remembering.
rows.anchor: ويقال في مصدره أيضا: ذكرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The renewed command after remembrance at the Sacred Monument intensifies the command; repetition often marks emphatic orders and here adds as He guided you.
rows.anchor: وإنما أعاد الأمر بالذكر بعد قوله: {فاذكروا الله عند المشعر الحرام} مبالغة في الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here qaḍaytum means performed: one has qaḍā what was owed by carrying it out; completion is its underlying sense.
rows.anchor: وأراد هاهنا: أديتم، لأنه يقال: قضى ما عليه، إذا أداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase when prayer is concluded refers to Friday prayer and cannot mean making it up instead of performing it.
rows.anchor: يعني: الجمعة، ولا يتصور فيها قضاء دون الأداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāsik may be the plural of mansak as a verbal noun like nusk, meaning the worship commanded in Hajj.
rows.anchor: والمناسك: جمع منسك الذي هو مصدر، بمنزلة النسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If manāsik is plural of a place of worship, the sense is completing the acts of the ritual places, with the annexed noun omitted.
rows.anchor: وإن جعلتها جمع منسك الذي هو موضع العبادة، كان التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes say Arabs recalled their fathers’ deeds and boasts after Hajj, so God ordered them to remember Him, who favored them and their fathers.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر أهل التفسير: كانت العرب إذا فرغوا من حجهم ذكروا مآثر آبائهم ومفاخرهم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says Arabs stood between the mosque at Mina and the mountain, listing their fathers’ virtues; God directs remembrance to monotheism and His blessings, since their fathers’ blessings came from God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: كانت العرب إذا قضت مناسكها وقفت بين المسجد بمنى وبين الجبل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s narration, Ibn Abbas holds that remembrance redirects ancestral boasts to God’s oneness and blessings.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء

rows.speaker: الربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: Another report compares remembering God to remembering both parents; fathers alone suffice in the wording, as in the verse about clothing that protects from heat.
rows.anchor: والضحاك (¬5): أراد: فاذكروا الله كذكركم آباءكم وأمهاتكم

rows.speaker: الربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: The authorities explain it as constantly mentioning the Lord in every state, like a young child who repeatedly says father and mother.
rows.anchor: أي: الهجوا بذكر ربكم في جميع أحوالكم، كما يلزم الصبي

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says Arabs commonly swore by their fathers, so God commands them to venerate Him as they venerated their fathers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري في هذه الآية: إن العرب كان أكثر أقسامها في الجاهلية بالآباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw ashadda dhikran means more strongly; its governor may be the kāf in ka-dhikrikum, putting it in genitive, or the verb udhkurū, putting it in accusative.
rows.anchor: يعني: وأشد (¬2)، والعامل فيه: الكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commanded remembrance is said to be takbir during the days at Mina, or supplication to God at those places.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذكر المأمور به هو التكبير أيام منى، وقيل: إنه الدعاء لله عز وجل

words: فمن الناس من يقول ربنا آتنا في الدنيا
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies these people as polytheists asking for wealth, livestock, rain, victory, and worldly expansion, without an afterlife share because they disbelieved in it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هم المشركون، كانوا يسألون المال والإبل والغنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of ātinā is omitted because it is understood: they ask for what worldly life can provide.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول {آتنا} من الكلام، وهو المسؤول من الدنيا؛ للعلم

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب ومعاذ بن جبل وسعد بن أبي وقاص
rows.claim: The verse was revealed after Umar, Muʿadh, Saʿd, and others asked the Prophet about wine and gambling, saying they impair reason and take wealth.
rows.anchor: نزلت في عمر بن الخطاب ومعاذ بن جبل وسعد بن أبي وقاص وجماعة، أتوا رسول الله

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists derive khamr from covering because wine veils the intellect.
rows.anchor: والخمر عند أهل اللغة سميت خمرا لسترها العقل

rows.speaker: ابن المظفر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Muzaffar defines khamr, its ripening and boiling, its maker, and the veil affecting a drunk person.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المظفر: الخمر معروف، واختمارها: إدراكها وغليانها، ومخمرها: متخذها

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says one says ikhtamartu khamran, but not akhmartuha.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: اختمرت خمرا، ولا يقال: أخمرتها

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab transmits that khāmir can mean one who conceals testimony; the root sense is covering, also reflected in the Prophetic instruction to cover vessels.
rows.anchor: روى ثعلب عن عمرو عن أبيه (¬5) قال: الخامر: الذي يكتم شهادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khamr can mean a place or thing that conceals someone, such as trees or a mound; khāmiri umm ʿāmir means go into hiding.
rows.anchor: أي: ادخلي الخمر، واستتري، والخمر: ما واراك من شجر

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Some say it is named for being covered until maturity; Ibn al-Anbari derives the name from mixing with the intellect, illustrated by poems about illness mixing with the heart.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سميت خمرا؛ لأنها تغطى حتى تدرك، وقال ابن الأنباري: سميت خمرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mixing derivation returns to covering, since what mixes with something becomes like a veil.
rows.anchor: وهذا (¬4) الذي ذكره راجع إلى الأول؛ لأن الشيء إذا خالط (¬5) الشيء يصير بمنزلة الساتر

rows.speaker: الثوري وأبو حنيفة وأكثر أهل الرأي
rows.claim: Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, and most jurists restrict khamr to grape or date juice that ferments naturally without fire; other drinks are not khamr.
rows.anchor: فمذهب الثوري (¬1) وأبي حنيفة وأكثر أهل الرأي (¬2): أن الخمر ما اعتصر

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأحمد وأهل الأثر
rows.claim: Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and hadith scholars define khamr as every intoxicating drink, from juice or infusion, cooked or raw; the author says Arabic supports this view.
rows.anchor: ومذهب مالك (¬5) والشافعي (¬6) وأحمد (¬7) وأهل الأثر (¬8): أن الخمر كل شراب مسكر

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj argues by analogy that anything producing wine’s effect should be called wine and share its prohibition; consensus forbids all gambling though the verse names the camel-lottery form.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: القياس أن ما عمل عمل الخمر أن يقال لها خمر

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says every intoxicant that mingles with and veils reason counts as wine; the Prophet’s hadith lists drink sources and bans every intoxicant.
rows.anchor: وأنا أنهاكم عن كل مسكر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet lists intoxicants made from dates, grapes, raisins, wheat, barley, and corn, then prohibits every intoxicant.
rows.anchor: إن من التمر لخمرا، وإن من العنب لخمرا، وإن من الزبيب لخمرا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Maysir means gambling; Ibn Abbas says a pre-Islamic man wagered his family and property, which the loser surrendered.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {والميسر} يعني: القمار، قال ابن عباس: كان الرجل في الجاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir is a mafʿil from yasara, to become due; yāsir is one whose lot or wager becomes due, then the terms meant gambling and gambler.
rows.anchor: والميسر عند أهل اللغة: مفعل، من قولهم: يسر لي هذا الشيء

rows.speaker: طرفة
rows.claim: Ṭarafa’s verse uses aysār as the plural of yusr for participants in the lot-based camel gamble.
rows.anchor: قال طرفة: وهم أيسار لقمان إذا

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrabi explains yasara al-yāsir as bringing one’s arrow to gamble.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأعرابي: يقال: يسر الياسر ييسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation links maysir to division and sharing; yasaru means to divide, illustrated by a poem about dividing the speaker like a camel’s limbs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أخذ الميسر من التجزئة والاقتسام (¬3)، ويقال: يسروا الشيء، أي: اقتسموه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs slaughtered a camel, divided it into shares, and gambled over them using arrows.
rows.anchor: يتقامر عليها بالقداح، على عادة لهم في ذلك

rows.speaker: النضر
rows.claim: Al-Nadr says yāsir means butcher and yasarat al-nāqa means she divided the camel’s meat; al-Aʿsha uses yāsir for butcher.
rows.anchor: قال النضر: الياسر: الجزار، ويسرت الناقة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: A further derivation takes maysir from ease because people shared a camel to make its cost easier; Muqatil says they asked to split its price.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب مقاتل؛ لأنه قال: (¬4) سمي ميسرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse is not the prohibition of wine and gambling; the prohibiting verse is in al-Maʾida.
rows.anchor: وليست هذه الآية المحرمة للخمر {والميسر} (¬6) إنما المحرمة التي في المائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sin includes quarrels, insults, obscene and false speech, loss of reason, and missing prayer; gambling breeds hostility when one takes another’s money without compensation.
rows.anchor: أراد: الإثم بسببهما من المخاصمة والمشاتمة، وقول الفحش

rows.speaker: الربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ and al-Dahhak say the sin became great after prohibition, while benefits existed before it.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع (¬1) والضحاك (¬2): إثم كبير بعد التحريم، ومنافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the first account: benefits meant wine profits and trade, pleasure and strength, and gambling winnings supporting the poor.
rows.anchor: عنى بالمنافع ما كانوا يصيبونه من المال في بيع الخمر

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s poem contrasts daytime wine’s sickness and sadness with evening pleasure and earnings.
rows.anchor: كقول الشاعر (¬4) الأعشى: لنا من ضحاها خبث نفس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the verse condemned wine and gambling without prohibiting them, since they were still lawful then.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: في هذه الآية ذمها ولم (¬7) يحرمها، وهي يومئذ حلال

rows.speaker: قوم من أهل النظر
rows.claim: Some rationalists argue wine was prohibited here because another verse prohibits sin generally and this verse calls wine and gambling sinful.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم من أهل النظر: إلى أن الخمر حرمت بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read kathīr with thāʾ; the other readers read kabīr with bāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ حمزة والكسائي (كثير) بالثاء، الباقون بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ reading is preferable because kabīr contrasts with small and other verses call grave sins kabāʾir; wine and gambling are major sins.
rows.anchor: وحجتهم: أن الباء أولى؛ لأن الكبر مثل العظم، ومقابل الكبر الصغر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ reading is supported by using ṣaghīr for small, not qalīl for few, and by the contrast of small with great; readers agree on bāʾ in the comparison phrase.
rows.anchor: وقالوا في اللمم: صغير وصغيرة، ولم يقولوا: قليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thāʾ reading is supported by the many sins in the wine-and-gambling verse.
rows.anchor: وأما من قرأ بالثاء فلأنه قد جاء فيهما ما يقوي (4) وصف الإثم فيهما بالكثرة دون الكبر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet cursed ten in connection with wine; sin is thereby abundant and may be called much.
rows.anchor: ولأن (5) النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - لعن عشرة في سبب الخمر

rows.speaker: عمرو بن الجموح
rows.claim: After the answer about parents and kin, ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh asked how much to spend, prompting revelation of say, the surplus.
rows.anchor: نزل في سؤال عمرو بن الجموح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, Qatada, and ʿAta say al-ʿafw is wealth left after providing for dependents.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية مقسم: العفو: ما فضل من المال عن العيال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the al-Walibi report, Ibn Abbas defines al-ʿafw as what is not conspicuous in one’s property.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الوالبي: ما لا يتبين (¬1)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says al-ʿafw is charity given from sufficiency.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: صدقة عن ظهر غنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿafw means increase; the verse until they grew and a poem about fat camels illustrate abundance.
rows.anchor: وأصل العفو في اللغة: الزيادة، قال الله تعالى: {حتى عفوا}

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes say people were told to give surplus, keeping a year’s expenses; obligatory zakat later abrogated this verse and earlier charity commands.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التفسير: أمروا أن ينفقوا الفضل، وكان أهل المكاسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers pronounce al-ʿafw accusative or nominative; with mā-dhā as one interrogative, it is object and the answer is accusative.
rows.anchor: فمن نصب جعل (ماذا) اسما واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With mā plus relative dhā, the question means what thing do they spend, and al-ʿafw is the nominative answer.
rows.anchor: ومن رفع العفو جعل ذا (¬4) بعد (ما) بمنزلة الذي، ورد العفو عليه فرفع

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq allows accusative al-ʿafw as the object of yanfiqūn and also allows nominative if mā-dhā is one word.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: ويجوز أن تنصب {العفو} وإن كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thus points to the explanation of spending: just as He explained al-ʿafw, God clarifies signs so people reflect and know the afterlife is superior.
rows.anchor: أشار إلى ما بين في الإنفاق، كأنه قال: مثل الذي بينه لكم في الإنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes thus as referring to God’s clarification about wine and gambling.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مثل البيان في الخمر والميسر يبين الله لكم الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular demonstrative is addressed to a plural because a group is grammatically treated as a tribe or collective.
rows.anchor: وهو يخاطب جماعة؛ لأن الجماعة معناها القبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾan uses a singular demonstrative for a plural group, as in the address to the Prophet’s wives followed by that is easy for God.
rows.anchor: الأصل: (ذلكن) (¬6)، إلا أن الجماعة في معنى القبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively the kāf addresses the Prophet alone; addressing him includes his community, as in the verse O Prophet, when you divorce women.
rows.anchor: وجائز أن يكون الكاف للنبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، أي: كذلك أيها النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means because God gave him kingship: the man disputed with Abraham because of the dominion, which made him arrogant.
rows.anchor: أي: لأن أتاه الله، وتأويله: ألم تر إلى الذي حاج إبراهيم في ربه للملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Abraham spoke, he answered an unstated question, namely who is your Lord? The answer makes the question understood and it is omitted.
rows.anchor: هذا جواب سؤال سابق غير مذكور، وتقديره (¬3): إذ قال له: من ربك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The enemy shifts to verbal equivocation, substituting ordinary killing and sparing for God’s creative power to give life and death.
rows.anchor: اعتمد عدو الله على المعارضة على الإشراك (¬7) في العبادة (¬8) في العبارة، عادلا عن وجه الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed report says the king summoned two men, killed one and spared the other, then called sparing the man giving life.
rows.anchor: لأنه روي أنه دعا برجلين؛ فقتل أحدهما واستحيا الآخر، فسمى ترك القتل إحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers omit the alif of ana in connected recitation; only a report from Nafiʿ retains it before hamza, and the author calls omission correct.
rows.anchor: عند الوصل في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun’s letters are hamza and nūn; its alif is added only in pause, like pausal hāʾ, and drops in connection as with hamzat al-waṣl.
rows.anchor: لأن (أنا) ضمير المتكلم، والاسم الهمزة والنون، فأما الألف فإنما تلحقها في الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafiʿ’s connected alif is very weak because it treats connection as pause; such forms are poetic necessities, not appropriate in Qurʾanic recitation.
rows.anchor: وأما قراءة نافع فهي ضعيفة جدا (¬8)، لأنه أجرى الوصل مجرى الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets extend pause forms into connected speech for meter or rhyme, as in the pausal hāʾ examples; this license does not apply outside poetry.
rows.anchor: الهاء فيه هاء الوقف التي تلحق في: مسلمونه وصالحونه، فألحق الهاء حرف اللين

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s verse retains the alif of ana in connected speech, illustrating poetic license.
rows.anchor: فمما (¬1) جاءت ألف (أنا) مثبته فيه وصلا من الشعر قول الأعشى

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: A verse transmitted by al-Kisaʾi also retains the alif of ana as poetic license.
rows.anchor: وما أنشده الكسائي: أنا شيخ العشيرة فاعرفوني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further unnamed poem retains the alif of ana before a line break.
rows.anchor: وقول آخر: أنا عبيد الله ينميني عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham could have demanded that the king revive his victim, but instead ends the dispute with an unanswerable proof that exposes inability and models argument against equivocation.
rows.anchor: إنما انتقل إبراهيم من الحجة الأولى مع إمكانه أن يناقضه بأن يقول له: أحيي من قتلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the king objected that Abraham’s Lord should bring the sun from the west, he had seen Abraham survive the fire; another view says God prevented the objection to aid His prophet.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل: كان للنمرود أن يقول لإبراهيم: فليأت بها ربك من المغرب
